body: Moeller, Schlingemann and Stulz, 'Firm Size and the Gains from Acquisitions' (Journal of Financial Economics 73(2), 2004; ~2,490 citations), 12,023 US deals 1980-2001: the announcement return for small acquirers is about 2 percentage points higher than for large acquirers, regardless of payment or target type. Large acquirers' shareholders lose money in aggregate. 'Wealth Destruction on a Massive Scale?' (Journal of Finance 60(2), 2005; ~1,570 citations): in 1998-2001, acquiring-firm shareholders lost about $240 billion in announcement windows, driven by a few very large loss deals by firms with high valuations. Loughran and Vijh, 'Do Long-Term Shareholders Benefit From Corporate Acquisitions?' (Journal of Finance 52(5), 1997; ~1,410 citations), 947 deals 1970-89: in the five years after, stock mergers earned about -25% excess returns, while cash tender offers earned about +62%. Paying with overvalued stock is a signal that management thinks its shares are expensive. Replicated: the size effect and the payment-method effect are robust; overall average announcement returns are near zero, with heavy losses in big deals at market peaks. Use for us: (1) in India, treat large overseas cash acquisitions (Tata Steel-Corus 2007, Suzlon-REpower, Bharti-Zain) and stock- or QIP-funded roll-ups at high P/E as negative-base-rate events; (2) small bolt-on deals in the same industry by disciplined acquirers are the exception; (3) check deal size relative to the acquirer's market cap and whether deals cluster near cycle highs.
title: Acquirers: small ones gain, large ones destroy value ($240bn in 1998-2001), and stock-financed deals underperform for years (Moeller-Schlingemann-Stulz; Loughran-Vijh)
